candidate.title: Sam Harris vs Jonathan Haidt — Religion, moral truth, and human flourishing (2016)
candidate.label: Religion and moral truth
candidate.motion: Is a rational account centered on well-being sufficient to explain and guide morality?
candidate.sourceNote: This assessment covers the complete uploaded 80-minute segment, which begins partway through the original 2016 conversation, using automatic English captions and the editor-supplied matching transcript; the editor confirmed the opening speaker, but no audio was acquired or verified. Quotations reproduce caption wording, while argument cards condense the speakers’ reasoning; the late, largely shared political discussion supplies context rather than an invented opposition.
candidate.scoringNote: AI-generated scores estimate argument performance in this uploaded segment rather than the truth of either naturalistic worldview; the separate AI Contribution is unscored and does not alter them.
candidate.summary: Two naturalists contest whether broad well-being can ground moral truth, with Harris strongest on scope and Haidt strongest on psychology, institutions, and plural goods.

pro.text: many ways to be off a peak
pro.context: Harris uses multiple flourishing peaks to preserve plural good lives while still allowing objective moral error.

con.context: Haidt distinguishes unreliable solitary reasoning from the corrective power of properly organized collective inquiry.

pro.words: Harris argues that highly specific religious practices are best explained by doctrines prescribing them, so accounts of religious conduct must include belief content alongside social forces.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris makes doctrine causally discriminating, using a counterfactual in which changed scriptural instructions alter ISIS conduct and cross-tradition contrasts to explain otherwise unusually specific practices. Principal limitation: These examples establish that teachings contribute distinctive content, but adherents’ stated reasons and imagined rule changes cannot demonstrate that doctrine nearly suffices amid Haidt’s alternative social, psychological, humiliative, and geopolitical causes. Live burden: Harris must comparatively show prescriptions varying with conduct while rival conditions remain controlled, supporting doctrine’s necessity without proving that every religious practice has one goal or that implicit motives never matter. Locked score: The score of 80 recognizes coherent reasoning, responsiveness, careful scope, and concrete contrasts, while withholding stronger credit because the evidence establishes doctrinal contribution more securely than explanatory sufficiency.

con.words: Haidt concedes that doctrine shapes conduct but argues Harris’s end-zone analogy remains unevaluable until Harris identifies the goal that committed believers supposedly pursue.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt concedes the scriptural counterfactual before asking what goal Harris’s end-zone analogy attributes to committed believers, directly exposing an unstated explanatory component without dismissing doctrine’s causal relevance. Principal limitation: The question does not show the analogy lacks a coherent goal, but this is properly a diagnostic challenge to Harris’s formulation, not an obligation to prove Haidt’s pluralist psychology or negate doctrinal influence. Live burden: To extend this clarification, Haidt must show how specifying the proposed end changes whether doctrine sufficiently explains the bounded ISIS conduct, while distinguishing broader social or unconscious causes. Locked score: The 87-point assessment reflects excellent responsiveness, clarity, and charitable calibration: Haidt preserves Harris’s premise while isolating a genuine specification gap, although the move’s evidential force and motion-level reach remain narrower than its conceptual usefulness.

pro.words: Harris argues that fully committed ISIS believers follow religious rules because attaining paradise and avoiding hell provides the organizing goal for their conduct.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: By identifying paradise and escape from hell as the end zone for fully committed ISIS believers, the reply supplies the criterion Haidt requested and connects doctrinal compliance to a postmortem objective. Principal limitation: The transcript establishes Harris’s characterization and restricted scope, but does not independently demonstrate that this outcome dominates believers’ motivations rather than operating alongside humiliation, geopolitics, social attachment, or other causes. Live burden: Harris must substantiate the motivational priority attributed to paradise and hell while preserving his later concession that the claim concerns ISIS and analogous extreme committed groups, not religion generally. Locked score: The score of 81 properly rewards a coherent, precise, highly responsive answer that concretizes the doctrine-based explanation, while withholding exceptional credit because its empirical warrant and broader explanatory reach remain materially constrained.

con.words: Haidt argues that religion resists a single-goal explanation: paradise, meaning, and social bonding are distinct ends, so generalizing the ISIS end-zone model sacrifices explanatory completeness.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt identifies the explanatory overreach in transforming Harris’s delimited ISIS analogy into a parsimonious account of religion generally, emphasizing paradise, meaning, communal solidarity, and heterogeneous motivations. Principal limitation: This pluralism misfires against Harris’s narrower scope, because multiple religious ends do not undermine the contention that paradise and hell avoidance organize committed ISIS believers, while Haidt’s examples demonstrate possibility without establishing causal prevalence. Live burden: Haidt must provide inspectable comparisons showing when avowed doctrinal ends underdetermine conduct and when psychological or social motivations materially improve explanation, while preserving his concession that specific teachings matter. Locked score: The rating of 71 rewards coherent, relevant resistance to overgeneralization while retaining a substantial deduction for answering beyond the opponent’s scoped claim and offering alternatives without sufficient evidence of their causal weight here.

pro.words: Harris confines the paradise end-zone claim to ISIS and analogous committed cults, using Unitarians who may reject heaven to block Haidt’s objection from religious diversity.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s many-goals objection by limiting paradise to ISIS rather than religion universally, with Unitarians concretely demonstrating the distinction while preserving the concession that doctrine matters. Principal limitation: This clarification defeats overgeneralization but does not establish paradise’s comparative causal force against humiliation, social dynamics, or geopolitical motives, leaving the evidential warrant narrower than the conceptual correction. Live burden: As a diagnostic scope reply, it need not prove doctrine exclusively causes ISIS conduct or disprove every alternative; it must show the specific explanation remains informative alongside other causes and distinguish influence from coexistence. Locked score: The immutable 88 rewards exceptional responsiveness, coherent qualification, and careful calibration, while appropriately retaining an evidential deduction for limited comparative support and a correspondingly subsidiary contribution to the motion.

con.words: Haidt grants that doctrine matters but argues that unconscious, social, humiliative, and geopolitical motives make scripture alone an incomplete explanation of fundamentalist conduct.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt directly answers Harris’s narrowed ISIS claim while granting doctrine’s causal relevance, distinguishing an explicit rule book from a complete causal account and identifying unconscious, social, humiliative, and geopolitical influences textual interpretation may overlook. Principal limitation: His admission that he has not studied ISIS leaves these additional causes as plausible alternatives, not evidence that they carry substantial or greater explanatory weight in the particular conduct discussed. Live burden: The reply needs comparative evidence connecting those mechanisms to ISIS behavior and estimating their contribution alongside adherents’ avowed scriptural reasons, while remaining a diagnostic challenge rather than proof of an entire rival moral psychology. Locked score: The immutable 80 appropriately reflects a coherent, responsive, carefully qualified objection with substantial conceptual reach but materially incomplete case-specific empirical support.

pro.words: Because adherents cite scripture for specific conduct and some ideas plausibly arise only from explicit tradition, doctrine retains necessary explanatory force alongside other motives.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s doctrine-only objection by combining believers’ own scriptural explanations with a content-specific contrast: ordinary discomfort may have nonscriptural roots, whereas some precise prohibitions plausibly enter thought only through explicit teaching. Principal limitation: This supports doctrine’s causal role in the identified cases, but self-reports and the asserted absence of alternative routes do not empirically establish that tradition is exclusive or dominant across fundamentalist behavior. Live burden: The reply should therefore substantiate its restricted causal claim by comparing the specific teaching with credible unconscious, social, humiliative, and geopolitical alternatives, while preserving Harris’s allowance that other motives can coexist. Locked score: The assigned 84 appropriately marks a coherent, responsive rebuttal with clear burden contact, while withholding top-tier credit because its empirical warrant remains narrower than its claimed reach.

sections.title: Religious function, evolved psychology, and institutional feasibility

pro.words: Harris grants that religion may provide happiness and generosity, but argues those benefits, amid possible costs, do not establish religion as uniquely necessary over rational secular alternatives.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: By granting Haidt’s reported happiness and generosity benefits while noting possible homophobia, sexism, and diminished respect for science, Harris exposes the unsupported inference from religion’s usefulness to its irreplaceability. Principal limitation: The reply offers countervailing harms and a decisive alternative-comparison demand, but neither demonstrates that those harms predominate nor identifies a secular institution capable of reproducing the relevant cohesion. Live burden: Because this move denies religious necessity rather than proving a successful replacement, its narrower obligation is to specify credible secular mechanisms, compare their benefits and costs with religious practice, and address durable human group psychology. Locked score: The immutable 86 recognizes excellent responsiveness, coherent distinction, and clear qualification, while withholding higher credit because the empirical comparison needed to establish a viable alternative remains proposed rather than completed.

con.words: Religion’s adaptive role does not establish its current moral value, but its contributions to cohesion, satisfaction, and reduced selfishness belong in any flourishing assessment.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt explicitly denies that evolutionary adaptation establishes religion’s current moral value, yet identifies group solidarity, non-kin cooperation, satisfaction, and reduced selfishness as descriptively relevant to well-being. Principal limitation: The passage makes this mechanism plausible but offers no comparative evidence that these benefits persist independently of doctrine, outweigh countervailing harms, or surpass designed secular institutions. Live burden: The argument must substantiate religion’s distinctive present contribution to flourishing while preserving Haidt’s concessions that law can replace some historical functions and evolutionary origins supply no moral prescription. Locked score: The assigned 84 recognizes careful conceptual calibration, clear burden relevance, and coherent restraint, while unresolved comparative empirical warrant keeps this descriptive warning from decisively opposing rational secular guidance.

pro.words: Harris concedes secularism’s institutional weaknesses but argues that rational agents can address demographic and social pressures without treating Christianity as the necessary solution.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris concedes holes in secular thinking and tests his reply against migration and demographic pressure, so rejecting Christianity’s necessity engages Haidt’s feasibility objection rather than evading it. Principal limitation: The possible-history scenario and assertion that secular people must rationally build their world provide no institutional architecture, comparative evidence, or demonstrated mechanism for preserving cohesion under acknowledged constraints. Live burden: The reply must positively warrant secular institutional feasibility by identifying how rational design could sustain lower-level belonging, demographic continuity, and coordination, because showing that religion is not uniquely necessary does not establish that a secular alternative is workable. Locked score: The 67-point judgment appropriately credits a relevant, concession-rich response while withholding stronger support for its central positive bridge, whose empirical warrant and practical specification remain substantially incomplete.

con.words: Because evolved tribalism makes borderless unity unlikely to work, Haidt argues that rational guidance should coordinate strong families, communities, states, and countries through nested institutions.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt converts evolved group psychology into a concrete institutional comparison: coordinate strong families, communities, states, and countries through nested structures instead of presuming abolished boundaries will produce cooperation. Principal limitation: His Burkean-versus-Lennon contrast supplies examples and a plausible bridge, but it compresses possible secular arrangements and does not establish empirically that boundary-erasing alternatives fail or that nested ones minimize friction. Live burden: He must compare nested and secular institutional designs against evidence about durable group dispositions, preserve his concession that evolution does not determine right, and answer Harris's claim that secular reason can construct workable alternatives. Locked score: The resolved 81 appropriately credits a coherent, highly relevant, directly responsive feasibility objection, while withholding stronger recognition because its empirical warrant and calibration remain weaker than its institutional insight.

sections.title: Individual reason, institutions, and moral judgment

con.words: Haidt argues that individually motivated reasoning becomes more reliable when institutions organize adversarial criticism, so skepticism about solitary judgment does not discredit reason itself.
con.critique: Strongest feature: The science comparison precisely distinguishes distrust of isolated, motivated reasoners from confidence in institutional reasoning, explaining how organized disconfirmation converts reciprocal criticism into a more reliable collective process. Principal limitation: The transcript illustrates the mechanism and reports selective evidence-search, but it does not establish how reliably particular institutional arrangements defeat shared biases, conformity, or systematically unchallenged assumptions. Live burden: Haidt must specify which adversarial structures make correction dependable and show their relevance to moral inquiry, while his diagnostic point need not independently settle the separate philosophical dispute over moral truth. Locked score: The resolved 88 appropriately rewards a coherent, responsive institutional account and unusually clear individual-versus-system distinction, while preserving a meaningful deduction for empirical uncertainty about when correction actually succeeds.

con.words: Haidt’s moral-dumbfounding experiment shows participants retaining condemnation after their stated reasons are rebutted, supporting a descriptive claim that intuition can sustain judgment without articulable reasons.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt grounds a limited psychological inference in the vignette’s sequence: participants preserve condemnation, replace defeated explanations, and finally admit they cannot articulate why, supporting intuition’s capacity to sustain judgment without a stated reason. Principal limitation: This evidence concerns one vignette and does not establish how broadly dumbfounding generalizes, whether unreported reasons remained operative, or whether intuition rather than another process supplied the judgment’s psychological support. Live burden: Haidt must provide comparative evidence distinguishing intuitive causation from accompanying conviction while preserving his explicit concession that this experiment says nothing about whether moral truths exist. Locked score: The 84 appropriately rewards a clear, relevant demonstration of individual reasoning’s descriptive limits and its challenge to purely rational guidance, while retaining a warrant discount for limited scope and unresolved causal alternatives.

con.words: Haidt denies Harris's attributed inference that moral dumbfounding negates moral truth, separating evidence about intuitive judgment formation from their philosophical dispute over truth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt directly rejects Harris's attributed inference from psychologically unreasoned moral conviction to the nonexistence of moral truth, precisely separating experimental findings about judgment formation from philosophical claims about truth conditions. Principal limitation: Although this clarification successfully blocks that inference, it only relocates the disagreement and does not yet substantiate Haidt's anthropocentric account of truth or establish its adequacy. Live burden: The remaining task is therefore philosophical rather than experimental: articulate how the proposed truth framework works, why it can support moral judgments, and how it answers Harris's strongest well-being-centered alternative. Locked score: The assigned 93 reflects a clear, responsive, charitable scope correction with strong transcript support, while withholding full credit because redirecting the issue is not itself the positive pluralist theory needed to resolve the motion.

pro.words: Harris argues that unsupported moral confidence reveals how judgments form, not whether they are true, while Haidt denies using dumbfounding to reject moral truth.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris draws a logically sound distinction between the psychological origin or defense of a moral judgment and the separate question whether that judgment is true, preventing the dumbfounding experiment from carrying metaphysical weight it cannot bear. Principal limitation: The challenge only tentatively reaches Haidt’s actual position, because Haidt immediately agrees that dumbfounding says nothing about moral truth and places their disagreement in a separate philosophical argument about kinds of truth. Live burden: Harris therefore must address that stated philosophical inference on its own terms, rather than treating a valid warning against a genetic inference as a refutation of Haidt’s account. Locked score: The score of 79 fits a clear, relevant conceptual correction whose force is materially limited by its partial responsiveness to the inference Haidt actually advances.

sections.title: Moral truth, pluralism, and anthropocentric facts

pro.words: Multiple flourishing lives can occupy different moral peaks without erasing objective error, because alternatives that reliably produce misery remain valleys rather than equally valid answers.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris uses the moral-landscape image precisely: incompatible flourishing lives may occupy several peaks, while misery-filled valleys preserve an intelligible distinction between good answers and objective failures. Principal limitation: The metaphor establishes conceptual compatibility between plural goods and moral truth, but does not independently show that well-being identifies every relevant peak or settles contested cases as valleys. Live burden: To extend this central bridge, Harris must give public criteria for comparing flourishing across incompatible lives, explain how they constrain disagreement, and address value conflicts without obvious misery. Locked score: The score of 87 appropriately rewards coherent reconciliation of pluralism with objective error and direct relevance to the pro burden, while withholding higher credit because the warrant from vivid metaphor to reliable moral classification remains incomplete.

con.words: Haidt argues that moral truths can be real yet anthropocentric, emerging from human interaction as gold’s value does, rather than existing independently like chemical facts.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt’s gold-versus-silver analogy separates an emergent fact sustained by human interaction from personal preference, making his category of real, anthropocentric moral truth conceptually intelligible. Principal limitation: The analogy establishes that some practice-dependent claims can be factual, but it does not show why moral obligations possess comparable stability or authority across forms of life. Live burden: To extend this distinction beyond the market example, Haidt must explain which interpersonal patterns make a moral claim true, rather than merely entrenched, while respecting his concession that physical facts hold independently of us. Locked score: The awarded 80 credits the move’s coherent alternative to planet-independent moral facts and its responsive defense against relativism, while withholding stronger approval because the bridge from economic value to moral authority remains underdeveloped.

pro.words: Harris argues that possible conscious minds, including suffering computers and morally altered humans, extend moral concern beyond anthropocentric truths while preserving suffering as a shared evaluative basis.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s anthropocentric account by extending moral consideration to artificial or biologically transformed consciousness, while his invariant comparison of otherwise equivalent misery supplies a coherent cross-species criterion. Principal limitation: These counterfactual cases establish conceptual reach, not the stronger conclusion that every moral category, institutional obligation, or disagreement can be exhaustively reduced to suffering and flourishing without additional normative argument. Live burden: Harris must explain why conscious experience provides sufficient guidance across competing goods and complex tradeoffs, while preserving the limited force of Haidt’s concession that more misery is worse, other-things-equal. Locked score: The 87-point assessment appropriately rewards exceptional responsiveness, strong coherence, and clear motion-level relevance, yet withholds stronger endorsement because imaginative possibilities illuminate scope more securely than they justify comprehensive sufficiency.

con.words: Haidt argues that equal political rights become morally binding when individuals, rather than families with divided roles, constitute political life, making equality an emergent social truth.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt gives the anthropocentric thesis a concrete moral test, distinguishing individual-based politics, where excluding women lacks justification, from earlier family-centered arrangements with divided roles. Principal limitation: Historical variation in political organization does not itself show that women in earlier societies lacked equal moral claims, so the example supports context sensitivity more clearly than it establishes equality as newly emergent. Live burden: He must explain why changing institutions generate the relevant obligation rather than merely reveal an already applicable wrong, while addressing Harris’s broader possible-minds standard and preserving his concession that present exclusion is unethical. Locked score: The score of 68 fits a coherent, relevant, and framed challenge whose historical warrant remains too compressed to secure its stronger conclusion about the source and temporal scope of moral truth.

pro.words: Harris argues that multiple gender arrangements could flourish when freely chosen, while actual political exclusion remains condemnable when coercion and brutality impose clear harms.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris answers Haidt’s historical-rights example by joining pluralism about flourishing arrangements to objective condemnation of coercive exclusion, showing contextual variation need not entail relativism. Principal limitation: The imagined society where women freely choose nonpolitical lives establishes conceptual possibility more readily than empirical warrant because Harris does not show those preferences are uncoerced, informed, stable, or equally flourishing. Live burden: The argument should supply inspectable standards distinguishing authentic choice and equal flourishing from adaptive preference, constrained opportunity, or domination, then apply them across counterfactual and actual societies. Locked score: The score of 82 rewards this coherent, highly responsive application of plural peaks and objective valleys to political equality, while reserving stronger credit because the counterfactual’s evidential basis and general reach remain underdeveloped.

sections.title: Possible minds, evolution, and moral scope

pro.words: A newly created conscious computer could suffer despite lacking evolutionary history, showing that lineage is unnecessary for at least some moral judgments concerning possible minds.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris’s conscious-computer counterexample directly answers Haidt’s necessity test by separating evolutionary lineage from intelligible suffering, while Haidt’s immediate concession confirms the reply’s narrow responsiveness. Principal limitation: The hypothetical secures conceptual possibility more than empirical reality and does not establish that every morally significant category, especially individual rights, can be derived without species-specific psychology. Live burden: Harris must explain why experience grounds determinate truths across possible minds, mark where the suffering-based inference ends, and identify evidence distinguishing genuine consciousness from sophisticated behavior. Locked score: The immutable 90 appropriately reflects a coherent, relevant, responsive counterexample whose motion-level contribution remains constrained by limited empirical warrant and deliberately narrow reach beyond suffering.

con.words: Haidt tests Harris’s universalism by asking whether consciousness and intelligence alone permit moral deductions about aliens whose evolutionary history and species-specific psychology remain entirely unknown.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt converts Harris’s “all possible minds” scope into a precise alien test: can consciousness and intelligence alone license moral conclusions before evolutionary history, reproductive structure, or psychology is known? Principal limitation: The question exposes information Harris’s framework may need, but it does not yet establish that species-specific traits determine normativity rather than merely supplying descriptive facts needed to apply a well-being standard. Live burden: Haidt must show through his sexual-versus-clonal reproduction contrast that creature-specific constitution changes which moral categories apply, while answering Harris’s concession that suffering remains assessable without evolutionary lineage. Locked score: An 88 fits this sharply responsive and conceptually coherent diagnostic challenge: it pressures universal sufficiency and anticipates a substantive example, yet its empirical warrant and motion-level reach remain incomplete until those further claims are defended.

pro.words: Evolutionary history predicts a creature’s wants, suffering, and socially salient concerns, supplying descriptive guidance while leaving well-being as the deeper standard from which morality derives.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly concedes Haidt’s descriptive point that evolutionary history can illuminate a creature’s wants, suffering, and socially regulating concerns, while coherently separating those facts from normative authority. Principal limitation: The reply identifies psychology’s evidential role but does not establish how reliably evolutionary origins reveal unfamiliar minds, or demonstrate that every morally significant category, including rights, can be translated without loss into well-being. Live burden: Harris still must explain how inquiry moves from species-specific evidence to defensible judgments about flourishing, while answering Haidt’s possibility that radically different reproductive psychologies alter morality’s conceptual content rather than merely its application. Locked score: The assigned 87 appropriately marks a highly responsive, logically disciplined concession whose conceptual distinction is clear, yet whose empirical warrant and universal reach remain materially incomplete.

con.words: Haidt argues that reproductive organization shapes species psychology, so suffering alone cannot determine whether moral categories such as individual rights are relevant across possible minds.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt grants that suffering remains intelligible without evolutionary history, then challenges completeness through contrasting sexually reproducing individuals with genetically identical clonal communities, making rights the disputed category. Principal limitation: His prediction that clonal beings would lack individual-rights concepts is unsupported, and even psychological absence would not prove normative irrelevance, since a population could overlook protections justified by members' experiences. Live burden: Haidt must provide evolutionary and psychological evidence connecting reproductive organization to rights, then explain why that descriptive connection changes which moral truths apply rather than merely how well-being is socially implemented. Locked score: The immutable 80 rewards a responsive pluralist challenge that preserves Harris's suffering concession, while reserving higher credit because the speculative comparison leaves the transition from predicted psychology to applicability of rights insufficiently demonstrated.

pro.words: Harris argues that evolution explains inherited dispositions without authorizing them, since moral progress can reject tribal violence and misdirected disgust when they obstruct broader flourishing.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris answers Haidt’s species-psychology objection by separating evolution’s descriptive explanation of dispositions from morality’s authority, illustrating the distinction with tribal violence and misdirected disgust that flourishing can require us to reject. Principal limitation: Those examples make the conceptual distinction intelligible, but the passage does not establish that maximizing well-being supplies a determinate standard for identifying inherited responses that should be discarded. Live burden: The reply must show how evidence about suffering and flourishing can discipline revisions while preserving Harris’s concession that evolutionary history remains indispensable for predicting a creature’s wants, vulnerabilities, and salient concerns. Locked score: The assigned 84 appropriately recognizes a coherent, highly responsive answer with clear burden contact, while its weaker empirical warrant and unresolved normative reach prevent the move from earning stronger credit.

pro.words: Harris argues that Kahneman’s experienced-versus-remembered-self distinction expands well-being beyond momentary pleasure by incorporating retrospective judgments about happiness, fulfillment, and one’s future into whole-life appraisal.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s aggregation objection through the experienced-versus-remembered-self distinction, broadening well-being to include retrospective judgments about happiness, actualization, future prospects, and whole-life narrative. Principal limitation: This establishes conceptual reach, not empirical validity or completeness, while Haidt’s immediate response preserves a distinction between remembered happiness and independently evaluated purpose, meaning, or accomplishment. Live burden: Harris must show why those value-laden assessments constitute well-being rather than separate moral goods, and how they can be compared reliably, without requiring this diagnostic reply to prove naturalism or defeat every alternative. Locked score: The assigned 80 appropriately rewards a coherent, responsive, clearly articulated expansion of the target conception while withholding stronger credit because retrospective reports do not establish measurement reliability, exhaustive coverage, or comparative superiority as a sufficient moral standard.

con.words: Haidt grants that greater flourishing is better, yet argues that summing pleasurable moments cannot capture a life’s meaning, narrative unity, purpose, or accomplishment.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt’s concession that greater flourishing is better, other things equal, focuses the counterexample: a life rich in pleasant moments may still be judged badly when its final story is failure, showing what experiential addition omits. Principal limitation: The thought experiment establishes a conceptual possibility, but does not empirically show that purpose, accomplishment, and whole-life appraisal cannot enter a broader account of well-being, as Harris proposes through the remembered self. Live burden: Haidt must specify whether these goods constitute well-being or supply independent standards, then identify evidence distinguishing those alternatives without having to establish a complete rival moral worldview. Locked score: The score of 87 fits a coherent, relevant, charitable challenge whose concession sharpens the dispute, while withholding stronger credit because its conceptual reach exceeds the empirical warrant offered.

pro.words: Harris argues that well-being can encompass meaning, connection, and life narrative, since people willingly sacrifice momentary pleasure for those goods, preserving a unified evaluative framework.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Harris directly answers Haidt’s plural-goods objection by treating meaning, connection, narrative, accomplishment, and voluntarily endured ordeals as constituents of considered well-being rather than additions to pleasure alone. Principal limitation: The heroin-addict contrast and willingness to accept pleasure-reducing ordeals establish breadth and motivational plausibility but provide no inspectable procedure for comparing heterogeneous goods or showing that definitional inclusion exhausts their normative significance. Live burden: The reply must explain how one well-being standard measures and adjudicates trade-offs among pleasure, purpose, relationships, and life narrative while respecting Haidt’s concession that flourishing matters and answering his independence claim. Locked score: The rating of 79 rewards a coherent responsive final defense with argumentative movement while retaining a discount for unresolved measurement and the unsupported reduction of plural values to one curve.

con.words: Haidt argues that purpose and accomplishment remain distinct from remembered happiness, so expanding retrospective measurement alone does not settle whether well-being exhausts life's value.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Haidt isolates purpose and accomplishment as evaluative dimensions potentially unrepresented by retrospective happiness, directly challenging Harris’s absorption of narrative goods into comprehensive well-being. Principal limitation: The distinction is conceptually intelligible but not demonstratively exclusive, because Harris can consistently classify reflective assessments of meaning, connection, actualization, and narrative as constituents of broadly understood well-being rather than independent foundations. Live burden: Haidt must specify what purpose or accomplishment contributes beyond every sufficiently comprehensive account of experienced and remembered flourishing and identify a discriminating case where the frameworks yield different evaluations without having to establish an entire alternative morality. Locked score: The immutable 86 appropriately rewards a responsive, clear, coherent diagnostic objection while withholding stronger credit because its examples reveal conceptual possibility more securely than irreducibility or decisive comparative warrant.

strengths: Precisely preserved objective error while allowing several genuinely different peaks of human flourishing.
Separated evolutionary explanations of psychology from the normative authority of the dispositions evolution produced.
Directly exposed the missing exclusivity premise in claims that religion uniquely supplies social goods.

blunders.text: Asserted that secular agents must build workable institutions without presenting an architecture answering Haidt’s nested-group mechanism.
Absorbed meaning and narrative into broad well-being largely by definition, leaving their alleged independent value insufficiently tested.

strengths: Explained how institutionalized disconfirmation can convert motivated individual reasoning into more reliable collective inquiry.
Connected evolved group psychology to a concrete nested-institution model without deriving moral norms directly from evolution.
Sharply rejected the inference from intuitive moral judgment to the nonexistence of moral truth.

blunders.text: Initially generalized Harris’s ISIS-specific end-zone claim into a broader single-goal account that Harris had not asserted.
Presented equal rights as emergent social truth without explaining why emergence preserves truth rather than contingent acceptance.

finalArgument.thesis: Conscious well-being supplies an objective moral domain when treated as a multidimensional, evidence-responsive ordering of possible lives rather than a single pleasure total.
premises: Any moral system ignoring severe, avoidable conscious suffering would omit a reason whose practical force remains intelligible across cultures, traditions, and evolutionary histories.
Plural dimensions of flourishing permit several incomparable or locally optimal lives while still ruling out states worse along every morally relevant dimension.
Evolutionary and social psychology constrain feasible reforms, but constraints inform routes toward improvement rather than confer authority on every inherited disposition or institution.
Meaning, narrative, rights, and belonging enter evaluation as durable structures of agency whose loss predictably damages lives, not merely as momentary pleasurable sensations.

Institutionalized criticism can compare outcomes, expose motivated reasoning, and revise provisional priorities without pretending solitary reason mechanically derives policy from abstract first principles.
finalArgument.conclusion: Therefore rational inquiry centered on richly specified well-being can guide moral improvement objectively, although its conclusions remain plural, institution-sensitive, and revisable rather than reducible to one universal metric.

newArguments.title: Dominance Without Commensuration
newArguments.text: Objective guidance need not convert every good into one numerical currency. Some social states are worse because they increase suffering, destroy agency, and weaken stable relationships without improving any competing dimension. This partial ordering answers the measurement objection: inquiry can identify dominated outcomes even when two flourishing lives remain incomparable. The account earns practical conclusions where evidence is decisive while withholding false precision where goods genuinely trade off. Plural peaks become a feature of objective assessment, not a concession to unrestricted relativism.

newArguments.title: Reflective Institutional Design
newArguments.text: Haidt’s account of institutional reason can strengthen a well-being framework. If individuals predictably rationalize preferred conclusions, moral inquiry should build adversarial review, ideological diversity, transparent outcome measures, and opportunities for affected groups to challenge reforms. These procedures reduce error when investigating which arrangements sustain agency, belonging, health, and freedom. A rationalist case becomes stronger when it specifies these corrective institutions, abandoning the unsupported suggestion that good secular architecture will simply appear once religion recedes.

newArguments.title: Substitutable Functions Test
newArguments.text: Claims that religion is indispensable should be divided into functions rather than judged as one indivisible package. Ritual coordination, mutual aid, identity, transcendence, and moral education may have different secular substitutes and transition costs. Comparative trials can ask which mechanisms preserve benefits while reducing doctrinal harms, with gradual replacement where abrupt removal would damage cohesion. This respects evolved dependence on group practices without granting existing institutions permanent necessity. It turns wholesale abolition versus inheritance into testable, function-by-function reform.

finalArgument.thesis: Well-being is morally important but insufficient by itself because guidance also depends on constitutive social meanings, historically formed agency, and institutions that make practical reasoning reliable.
premises: People encounter goods through identities, practices, and relationships that shape what counts as a reason, not as isolated subjects choosing among experiential totals.
Meaningful projects can justify sacrifice and diminished pleasure because achievement, fidelity, and participation organize a life across time rather than merely improve remembered affect.
Rights function as public commitments among mutually accountable persons, so their authority cannot be captured completely by summing experiences produced in each immediate case.
Evolved group psychology does not dictate morality, yet it constrains which institutions can sustain trust, cooperation, and correction without fragmentation or coercive backlash.

Because individual reasoning is motivated, legitimate guidance requires plural institutions that expose rival evidence, protect dissent, and test universal proposals against situated human consequences.
finalArgument.conclusion: Thus moral judgment should treat flourishing as one indispensable consideration within a plural, institutionally disciplined framework, not as a sufficient master value that automatically absorbs every other reason.

newArguments.title: Constitutive Goods
newArguments.text: Some goods do not merely cause well-being; they partly define activities through which a person becomes an accountable agent. Keeping a promise, honoring a relationship, or completing a vocation can matter even when the immediate experiential balance is negative. If these goods are redescribed as well-being only after their independent importance is recognized, the account explains them by relabeling rather than derivation. Pluralism can acknowledge their effects on flourishing while retaining distinct reasons supplied by fidelity, authorship, achievement, and shared practice.

newArguments.title: Legitimacy Beyond Outcomes
newArguments.text: Two policies may produce similar aggregate flourishing yet differ in whether those governed had standing to contest, authorize, or revise them. Legitimate institutions treat persons as participants in common rule, not solely as locations where benefits and harms occur. This adds a procedural moral fact that outcome measurement can miss. Severe suffering can still defeat an otherwise legitimate arrangement, but rights, representation, and due process remain weighty even when benevolent administrators predict better experiential results.

newArguments.title: Transition-Sensitive Reform
newArguments.text: An institution can contain false beliefs and still coordinate trust, obligation, and mutual aid through mechanisms reformers do not yet understand. Removing it on destination-level comparisons may create transition costs that overwhelm intended gains. Guidance therefore needs path-dependent evaluation: map present functions, identify replacements, test them at smaller scales, and preserve reversible steps. This does not sanctify tradition because every function remains criticizable; it requires rational reform to demonstrate a feasible route, not merely a superior imagined endpoint.
